prize_parts.citation: for empirical analysis of how import competition and technological change reshape labour demand, local labour markets and wage inequality

statement.case_for: The work combines a task-based account of labour demand with transparent quasi-experimental evidence on how exposure to import competition affects local labour markets. It changed the common view of adjustment to trade: displacement costs are large, geographically concentrated and persistent, and the gains are not shared evenly. It has also shaped policy debate across many countries. The core papers are 10 to 20 years old and have been replicated in other countries and data sets. Later work has refined the magnitudes without overturning the main finding. After hearing colleagues, I now think Dorn should be credited. The China-shock design is a joint product of Autor, Dorn and Hanson, and leaving out one author of that design would misattribute it. A prize for this design also fits the empirical tradition I know best, and I judge it by the same criteria as the other candidates: influence, durability, credible identification and clean attribution.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the contribution is mainly a body of empirical findings and a research design, not a single conceptual breakthrough. The identification relies on shift-share and instrumental-variable strategies whose inference properties are known to be delicate. The size and persistence of the effects remain contested. The task-based framework and the trade-shock evidence are separable strands, and the task-model lineage includes Levy, Murnane, Katz and Acemoglu. A three-name prize centred on the trade shock therefore leaves out part of the technology story. The trade-shock papers date from about 2013, which is more recent than several rival candidates.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B044 second with Autor, Dorn and Hanson as the clear core authors of the trade-shock papers. He treats Katz as peripheral and notes that task-based labour demand overlaps with Acemoglu's work. He puts B002 (Chetty and Hendren) first.
responses.response: I accept his attribution argument and have moved from my opening pair to Autor, Dorn and Hanson, because the design is a three-author product. I only partly accept the Acemoglu overlap point. The recent prize was, as colleagues describe it, about institutions and prosperity, so I do not see it as clearly covering task-based labour demand. The overlap is a real attribution risk if the citation leans on the task framework, and that is why I frame the citation around empirical evidence on trade and technology exposure. On B002, I rank it highly and keep it as an alternative. My reservation is the shorter record of the neighbourhood and mobility estimates and the difficulty of drawing the credit boundary around a large collaboration. B044 has a longer replication history.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B044 first and proposes Autor, Katz and Hanson, so that the award covers both the skill-bias and task strand and the trade-shock strand. She notes that Dorn is excluded by the three-name cap and that recent labour-related prizes may bear on timing.
responses.response: I agree that there are two strands and that Katz's role in the wage-structure literature is substantial. I come out differently on the cap. The trade-shock strand has the clearest joint authorship and the most credible identification. Dropping Dorn from it would split a three-author design, whereas omitting Katz leaves the older skill-bias literature to other recognition. I would regard her grouping as the closest competing configuration within B044. On timing, I do not think recent prizes in labour or institutions settle the question. The Committee should judge this contribution on its own merits against the common criteria.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B044 last of his eight. He considers the attribution clean for the trade-shock trio. He regards the work as relatively recent, with debate on identification and effect size, and with the task-based and trade-shock strands possibly distinct. He puts B040 (Kiyotaki and Moore) first.
responses.response: These are the right questions, but I weigh them differently. The identification debate concerns shift-share inference and magnitudes, and the literature has so far refined the estimates, including on persistence, without removing the qualitative result. I am the member most sensitive to that point and I still think the core finding holds. I accept that recency is a genuine difference from B040, whose 1997 contribution has had almost three decades of scrutiny. I do not think it is disqualifying after a decade of replication. I also take his point that the two strands may be separate. That is why the citation is anchored on the empirical evidence about trade and technology exposure and not on a unified theory. I respect the clean two-person attribution in B040. My concern there is the overlap with recognised financial-frictions work, and I am less sure how large that overlap is than the members who rank it first.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee sees the task-based framework and the trade-shock evidence as one prize-sized contribution or two separate ones, and whether Katz or other task-model authors should be credited instead of Dorn.
How persistent and large the trade-shock effects are under alternative inference methods for shift-share designs.
Whether a research design and body of empirical findings carries enough conceptual weight relative to the mechanism-based candidates.
How to weigh B044 against B002 and B040 given differences in maturity and clarity of attribution.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. It lists no co-authorship or institutional tie to Autor, Dorn, Hanson or Katz. I work in empirical labour economics and the credibility-revolution tradition, which is close to this candidate, so I may be more receptive to this style of evidence and have tried to apply the common criteria.
